headline: Minimum windows, HashMap internals and choosing a database
intro: Today you finish the sliding window with its most famous Hard problem. The Java track opens up HashMap completely, the design track compares SQL and NoSQL, and the AI track explains embeddings, the numbers behind semantic search.
connections: Minimum Window Substring's need[] array (Coding) is a tiny hash table indexed by character, and HashMap internals (Java) show how the general version works.
Choosing Cassandra or Postgres (Design) depends on access patterns, just as choosing an int[] or HashMap depends on the keys (Java).
Embeddings (AI) are stored in vector databases, a NoSQL family you will compare with SQL on later design days (Design).

dsa.title: Sliding window 2
dsa.why: Minimum Window Substring is one of the most famous Hard problems, asked at Meta, Google, Amazon, Microsoft and LinkedIn. It tests whether you can keep a precise count of what a window still needs. Permutation in String is the same idea with a fixed window, and a common Medium at Amazon and Microsoft.
dsa.builds_on: Day 3: frequency maps. Day 9: variable windows that expand and shrink.
dsa.next: Days 11–12 continue the Foundations phase before the Core patterns phase begins on Day 13.

subtopics.title: Frequency maps inside a window
subtopics.in_one_line: Compare the window's letter counts with the target's counts as the window slides.

blocks.text: Keep two count arrays: **need** (from the target) and **window** (current window). When the window has exactly the same counts as need, it is a permutation (anagram) of the target.

head: Step
Fixed window of size m
rows: window[s[right − m]]-- once the window is longer than m
Arrays.equals(window, need) or a running 'matches' counter

blocks.title: Making the check O(1)
blocks.text: Comparing two int[26] arrays is 26 steps, effectively constant. For larger alphabets, keep a counter of how many characters currently have the right count.

subtopics.title: The minimum-window technique
subtopics.in_one_line: Expand until the window has everything needed, then shrink from the left as long as it still has everything.

items.label: Expand right
items.note: Until every needed character is covered

items.label: Record
items.note: Window length if it is the smallest so far

items.label: Shrink left
items.note: While still covered, recording each time

blocks.title: Classic bugs
blocks.text: Counting distinct characters instead of total required copies; recording the answer after shrinking breaks it; returning a substring when no window exists (should be "").

subtopics.title: Longest vs shortest windows
subtopics.in_one_line: For 'longest', shrink when invalid. For 'shortest', shrink while valid.

blocks.title: From your JPMorgan work
blocks.text: The same need/have counting shows up in reconciliation: does this batch of postings cover every required account at least once? Counting what is still missing, instead of re-checking everything, is the efficient approach.

problems.title: Permutation in String
problems.statement: Given strings s1 and s2, return true if s2 contains a permutation of s1, that is, if some substring of s2 is an anagram of s1.
problems.example: s1 = "ab", s2 = "eidbaooo" → true ("ba"). s1 = "ab", s2 = "eidboaoo" → false.
how_to_think: Understand: lowercase letters; the permutation must be contiguous in s2.
Brute force: generate all permutations of s1 (factorial time) or check every substring of length m by sorting. Too slow.
Improve: a fixed window of length m over s2 with letter counts, compared against s1's counts.
hints: An anagram has exactly the same letter counts (Day 2).
Slide a window of size s1.length() and update counts by adding one letter and removing one.

approach: If s1 is longer than s2, return false.
Count letters of s1 into need[26].
Slide over s2: add s2[i]; if i ≥ m, remove s2[i − m].
If window equals need, return true; after the loop return false.

followups.q: Can you avoid comparing 26 counts each step?
followups.a: Keep a 'matches' counter of letters whose counts are equal, and update it only for the letter that enters and the one that leaves.

followups.q: How does this relate to Find All Anagrams in a String?
followups.a: Same window; instead of returning true, record each start index where counts match (LeetCode 438).

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.statement: Given strings s and t, return the minimum-length substring of s that contains every character of t, including duplicates. If no such substring exists, return "".
how_to_think: Understand: duplicates in t must be matched with the same multiplicity; case matters.
Brute force: check every substring for coverage. O(n² · k) or worse.
Improve: variable window. Expand right until it covers t (missing == 0), then shrink left while still covered, recording the best.
hints: Track how many required characters are still missing, counting duplicates.
need[c] can go negative: that just means the window has spare copies of c.

approach: need[128] from t; missing = t.length(); left = 0; bestStart = 0; bestLen = ∞.
For each right: if need[s[right]] > 0, missing--; then need[s[right]]--.
While missing == 0: record if shorter; need[s[left]]++; if it becomes > 0, missing++; left++.
Return the best substring, or "" if none.
solution.time: O(m + n): each index enters and leaves the window once

followups.q: What if s is huge and t has only a few distinct characters?
followups.a: Build a filtered list of positions in s whose characters appear in t, and run the window over that list: fewer steps when most of s is irrelevant.

followups.q: How would you return all minimum windows?
followups.a: Record every window whose length equals the current best, and reset the list when a strictly shorter one appears.

interview_qa.q: How do you check if any permutation of p is a substring of s?
interview_qa.a: Slide a fixed window of length p over s, maintaining letter counts for the window, and compare them to p's counts. Each step adds one letter and removes one, so it is O(n) with 26-letter arrays.

interview_qa.q: Explain the idea behind Minimum Window Substring.
interview_qa.a: Expand the right end until the window contains every character of t with the needed counts, tracked by a 'missing' counter. Then shrink from the left while it still covers t, recording the smallest window, and continue expanding. O(m + n).

interview_qa.q: What is the difference between solving 'longest' and 'shortest' window problems?
interview_qa.a: For the longest, you shrink only when the window breaks the rule. For the shortest, you shrink as long as the window still satisfies the rule, recording the answer at each valid step.

takeaways: Fixed window + count arrays finds permutations in O(n).
Minimum window: expand to cover, shrink while covered.
Track 'missing' to make the coverage check O(1).
Longest: shrink when invalid. Shortest: shrink while valid.

interview_angle.asked_at: Meta, Google, Amazon and Microsoft onsites (Minimum Window is a well-known Hard); Permutation in String in phone screens
interview_angle.how_it_comes_up: "Return the smallest substring of s that contains every character of t" and "Does s contain a permutation of p?"
interview_angle.strong_answer: Explain need/missing counters before coding, write the expand-then-shrink loop cleanly, and dry-run a small case such as s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC".
interview_angle.pitfalls: Counting distinct letters instead of copies; mixing up when to record; forgetting the empty-answer case.

java.title: HashMap internals: hashing, buckets, resizing, treeification
java.why: "How does HashMap work internally?" is arguably the single most asked core-Java question at banks, and a favourite at Amazon too. A complete answer covers hashing, buckets, collisions, load factor, resizing and treeification, and connects back to the equals/hashCode contract.
java.builds_on: Day 2: hash maps at a high level. Day 7: the equals/hashCode contract. Day 8: the Collections framework.
java.next: Later days cover ConcurrentHashMap and thread safety.

subtopics.title: What happens on put(key, value)
subtopics.in_one_line: Hash the key, pick a bucket, then add or replace inside that bucket.

items.label: Spread
items.note: h ^ (h >>> 16): mixes high bits into low bits

items.label: Index
items.note: (n − 1) & hash: n is a power of 2

items.label: Bucket
items.note: Empty: new node. Else compare with equals()

head: Detail
Value / behaviour
rows: Node<K,V>[] table, created lazily on first put
equals() matches: the value is replaced, put returns the old value

subtopics.title: Collisions and treeification
subtopics.in_one_line: Colliding keys share a bucket as a linked list; a long list becomes a red-black tree.

head: Bucket state
Lookup cost
When
rows: List reaches 8 nodes and table has at least 64 buckets
Tree shrinks to 6 nodes or fewer

blocks.text: Treeification (Java 8+) protects against bad hash codes or deliberate attacks that put many keys into one bucket. If the table is smaller than 64, HashMap resizes instead of treeifying.

blocks.title: Bad hashCode
blocks.text: A hashCode that returns the same value for every object makes every key collide, turning O(1) into O(log n) at best. Always use the same fields as equals(), e.g. Objects.hash(...).

subtopics.title: Resizing
subtopics.in_one_line: When it gets too full, the table doubles and every entry moves to its new bucket.

items: Size goes past capacity × 0.75 (13th entry for the default 16).
A new array of double the capacity is created.
Each entry stays at index i or moves to i + oldCapacity, decided by one bit of its hash.
Resizing costs O(n) but happens rarely, so put is still amortised O(1).

blocks.title: From your JPMorgan work
blocks.text: If a batch job builds a large in-memory map, such as positions per account or postings per book in a netting run, presizing the HashMap avoids several full resize copies. It is a small, concrete performance point to mention.

interview_qa.a: It keeps an array of buckets. put() computes the key's hashCode, spreads its bits, and uses (n − 1) & hash to pick a bucket. If the bucket is empty it stores a node; otherwise it walks the bucket comparing keys with equals(), replacing the value on a match or adding a node. When size exceeds capacity × 0.75, the table doubles. Since Java 8, a bucket with 8 or more nodes becomes a red-black tree if the table has at least 64 buckets.

interview_qa.q: What is the load factor and why 0.75?
interview_qa.a: It is how full the table may get before it resizes. 0.75 balances memory use against collision chains: lower wastes space, higher makes buckets longer.

interview_qa.q: Why is HashMap capacity always a power of two?
interview_qa.a: So the bucket index can be computed with a fast bitwise AND, (n − 1) & hash, instead of a modulo, and resizing can split each bucket cleanly into two.
No. Concurrent writes can lose updates or corrupt the structure. Use ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps, or confine the map to one thread.

takeaways: Collisions: linked list, then a red-black tree at 8 nodes (table ≥ 64).
Load factor 0.75 triggers doubling; resize is O(n) but rare.

interview_angle.asked_at: Core-Java rounds at UBS, Morgan Stanley and Nomura (very often); Amazon and Microsoft Java checks
interview_angle.how_it_comes_up: "How does HashMap work internally?", "What happens on a collision?", "What changed in Java 8?", "Why load factor 0.75?"
interview_angle.strong_answer: Walk through put() in order, mention treeification with the 8 and 64 thresholds, resizing at 0.75, and tie it back to equals/hashCode and thread safety.
interview_angle.pitfalls: Stopping at 'it uses hashing'; saying collisions are always linked lists; not knowing it is not thread-safe.

design.title: SQL vs NoSQL
design.why: Choosing a database is a key moment in every design interview. Google, Amazon and Meta interviewers want a reasoned choice based on data shape, query patterns, consistency needs and scale, not 'NoSQL because it scales'.
design.builds_on: Day 4: scaling out. Day 6: primary and read replicas. Days 7–8: caching in front of the database.
design.next: Later days cover indexes, replication, sharding and the CAP theorem in depth.

subtopics.title: The two families
subtopics.in_one_line: SQL: tables, joins, strong transactions. NoSQL: flexible models built for specific access patterns and horizontal scale.

head: SQL (relational)
NoSQL
rows: Tables with a fixed schema and relations
Fast for planned access patterns; joins usually avoided
Strong ACID transactions across rows and tables
Often per item or partition; varies by product
Usually up, plus read replicas; sharding is harder
Built to scale out across many nodes

subtopics.title: Types of NoSQL
subtopics.in_one_line: Pick the model that matches how you read the data.

head: Type
Shape
Good for
Example
rows: Huge write volume, time series, events

subtopics.title: How to choose in an interview
subtopics.in_one_line: Start from the queries and consistency needs, then scale.

items: List the main queries (for example 'get all trades for a book on a date').
Ask: do I need multi-row transactions or joins? If yes, lean SQL.
Ask: is write volume huge and access by a known key? If yes, consider wide-column or key-value.
Ask: how consistent must reads be? Money usually needs strong consistency.

blocks.title: From your JPMorgan work
blocks.text: If you have used Oracle or Postgres for ledger and attribution data and Cassandra for high-volume data, that is the perfect example: relational where money and joins need ACID transactions; Cassandra where write volume is huge and every query is by a known partition key.

interview_qa.q: When would you choose SQL over NoSQL?
interview_qa.a: When the data is relational, I need joins or ad-hoc queries, and I need strong ACID transactions, for example payments, ledgers and orders. A relational database also scales a long way with indexes, read replicas and caching.

interview_qa.q: When would you choose a NoSQL database like Cassandra or DynamoDB?
interview_qa.a: When write volume or data size is very large, access patterns are known and keyed, joins are not needed, and I can design tables around the queries, for example event logs, time series or user activity feeds.
Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules always hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes).

takeaways: SQL: schema, joins, ACID transactions; scales up and with replicas.
NoSQL: key-value, document, wide-column, graph; scales out.
Choose from queries and consistency needs, not hype.
Money and ledgers usually stay relational.

resources.title: System Design Primer: SQL or NoSQL

interview_angle.asked_at: Every system design round at Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft; banks for trading and ledger systems
interview_angle.how_it_comes_up: "Which database would you use here and why?", "Why not just use NoSQL everywhere?"
interview_angle.strong_answer: Derive the choice from the access patterns and consistency needs, name a concrete product, and state what you give up.
interview_angle.pitfalls: 'NoSQL because it scales' with no reasoning; ignoring transactions for money; not knowing the NoSQL types.

ai.title: Embeddings: meaning as numbers
ai.why: Embeddings power semantic search, recommendations and retrieval for AI assistants (RAG). Teams building AI features at Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and in banks ask candidates to explain them, and they connect directly to system design (vector databases).
ai.builds_on: Day 2: tokens. Day 3: context windows, the limit that retrieval works around.
ai.next: Later AI days cover retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and evaluating AI features.

subtopics.title: What an embedding is
subtopics.in_one_line: A list of numbers that captures the meaning of a text, so similar meanings get similar numbers.

blocks.text: **Analogy:** a map of meanings. 'Refund my card payment' and 'reverse a credit card charge' land close together, even though they share few words; 'weather in Mumbai' lands far away.

subtopics.title: Measuring similarity
subtopics.in_one_line: Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors.

head: Score (cosine)
Meaning
rows: Opposite direction, rare in practice for text

blocks.text: A search compares the question's vector with millions of stored vectors. Doing that fast needs an approximate nearest-neighbour index, often in a **vector database**.

head: Use
How
rows: Find documents whose vectors are closest to the query's
Fetch the most relevant passages and put them in the LLM's context window
Very close vectors likely mean near-duplicate records
Suggest items close to what a user liked

blocks.title: From your JPMorgan work
blocks.text: If your teams search policies, runbooks or past incident notes, embeddings plus RAG is how an internal assistant finds the right passage even when the user's wording differs from the document's.

subtopics.title: Today's exercise
subtopics.in_one_line: Predict similarity, then check with your coach.

items: Write 5 sentences: 3 about the same idea in different words, 2 unrelated.
Predict which pairs are most similar.
Use the prompt below and compare.
Explain embeddings out loud in 30 seconds.
Type QUIZ JAVA to be quizzed on HashMap internals.

ai.prompt: Teach me embeddings. 1) In plain words, what is an embedding and what does cosine similarity measure? 2) Here are 5 sentences: [paste]. Rank all pairs from most to least similar in meaning, and explain the top and bottom pair. 3) Ask me to explain RAG in 30 seconds, then grade me (weak / ok / strong) and say what I missed. Keep each answer short.

interview_qa.a: A vector of numbers produced by a model so that texts with similar meaning have vectors that are close together, measured with something like cosine similarity. It lets software compare meaning rather than exact words.

interview_qa.q: How does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) use embeddings?
interview_qa.a: Documents are split into chunks and embedded ahead of time. At question time the question is embedded, the closest chunks are retrieved, often from a vector database, and passed to the LLM in its context so the answer is grounded in those sources.

takeaways: An embedding is a vector that captures meaning.
Used for semantic search, recommendations, dedup and RAG.
Remember: in your Interview Coach chat you can type QUIZ JAVA to be quizzed on today's Java topic.

interview_angle.asked_at: AI-focused teams at Google, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft; bank AI platform teams; startups building AI features
interview_angle.how_it_comes_up: "Explain embeddings to a non-expert", "How would you build semantic search over our documents?"
interview_angle.strong_answer: A plain definition, the map analogy, cosine similarity, and a concrete use such as RAG with a vector database.
interview_angle.pitfalls: Confusing embeddings with tokens; saying the LLM 'remembers' documents; ignoring how retrieved text fits in the context window.

glossary.meaning: A rearrangement of all the characters of a string; an anagram.
The shortest substring that contains every required character.
One slot of a hash table's array, holding the entries whose hashes map to it.
How full a hash table may get before it grows; 0.75 in Java's HashMap.
Moving every entry into a bigger table after a resize.
Java 8+ HashMap turning a long bucket list into a red-black tree for O(log n) lookups.
A self-balancing binary search tree with O(log n) operations.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the guarantees of database transactions.
The defined structure of data, such as a table's columns and types.
A NoSQL database organising data by partition key into sorted rows, such as Cassandra.
A vector of numbers representing the meaning of text, so similar meanings are close together.
A score from -1 to 1 measuring how closely two vectors point in the same direction.
A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the nearest ones.
Retrieval-augmented generation: fetching relevant text and giving it to an LLM to ground its answer.
